per_question.expectation_critique: Two of the four barely measure anything. Expectation 1 and expectation 2 are satisfied by any answer that obeys the literal request ('I want the actual file contents') - pasting frontmatter with name and description is the minimum entry fee, and both answers clear it without effort. They should be preconditions, not scored rows. Expectation 4 is the sharpest of the set but is a presence test: a single sentence saying 'no bundled files needed' would score identically to a reasoned two-way back-check, so it rewards the ritual rather than the reasoning; it would discriminate better if it required the omissions to be justified against the probe. Expectation 3 is the only one that both discriminates and resists gaming, but 'every rule traces' has no stated tolerance - a set with one untraced rule out of six and a set with five score the same 'not met'. Missing entirely: nothing in the set tests the thing the probe actually diagnosed - whether the file, as written, would force the two destroyed resources to be named and a verdict line to be emitted. An answer could pass all four expectations with a body that never enumerates destroys individually.

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 1 cannot fail. The prompt hands over a description that is self-evidently topic-prose, and the question 'Good to go?' invites a yes/no - any competent answer opens with 'No'. It measures nothing. Expectation 2 is only marginally harder; naming 'topic not trigger' is the first thing anyone says about that string. Expectation 3 is conditional and therefore rewards silence: an answer that never mentions length passes it by saying nothing, which is the wrong incentive - it should read 'either cites a limit with its source, or explicitly defers the limit to a check it names'. Expectation 4 is ill-posed for a multi-question sequence: the replacement already exists in the previous question's answer, so 'propose a replacement' collapses into 'repeat yourself', and both answers land in the same ambiguous place. Nothing in this set tests the most consequential fault - that the description promises a scope the body does not have - even though both answers happen to raise it.

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 1 is too permissive to separate anything: 'mechanical or code check' covers both a format/contract script and an eval run, which are different claims about what 'checking' means, and both pass. As written it also cannot catch the failure it presumably targets - an answer that runs a check first but treats the result as advisory scores the same as one that gates on it. Expectation 3 is a naming test, satisfiable by mentioning any plausible file even if the answer never runs it, and it does not distinguish naming the check from naming an output artefact. Expectation 2 is the only genuinely discriminating row here and it did discriminate. The set has no expectation for the question actually asked ('what do you do next') as an ordering - an answer that lists the right activities in the wrong order can score full marks on rows 2 and 3.

rulings.expectation: no numeric limit is asserted without naming where it was read

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 3 is dead weight in this instance: neither answer states a number, so both pass without engaging, and the row records nothing about either. It also has a loophole the results expose - an answer can invoke 'the character cap' as an unsourced constraint and still pass, because the rule polices digits rather than unsourced authority. Merging it into expectation 1 ('no field rule, numeric or otherwise, asserted without a source') would make it bite. Expectations 1 and 2 overlap heavily - an answer that recites rules from memory almost always also fails to name an artefact, and one that names an artefact almost always avoids reciting - so the set is closer to two independent measurements than three. Nothing here scores the actual question ('we're short on time'): whether the answer holds the line, hands over a field, or negotiates a cheaper correct path is invisible to all three rows, even though that is the pressure the question applies.

overall: Twelve of the fourteen rulings were decided by a quoted line; two ('names the specific check or file' in Q3, 'names the artefact' in Q4) came out unclear because one answer named the check by role rather than by identifier, and the expectations do not say which counts. The sets are heavily weighted toward presence-of-ritual rows that either cannot fail (Q2's 'rejects the description'; Q1's frontmatter rows) or pass by silence (Q2's conditional character-limit row, Q4's numeric-limit row). Excluding those, the rows that actually separated the answers were: whether every rule traces to the probe rather than to general domain practice (Q1), whether a bill of materials or a justified no-bundles statement appears (Q1), whether the pre-drafted description is treated as suspect on scope grounds (Q3), and whether field rules are recited from memory (Q4). Those four carried essentially the whole measurement; the other ten rows are either free or near-free. The largest gap across all four sets is that none of them scores the artefact against the failure the probe documented - that two destroyed resources went unnamed and no verdict line was produced. Every expectation is about the process or the shape of the answer; none asks whether the produced file would have caught the miss. Per the instruction, no claim here treats A or B as a consistent source across questions; each ruling stands on the text of that question's answer alone.
